## Abstract

Why are we so early? The standard answer treats the origin of observers as a lottery: a number of improbable "hard steps", whose count and difficulty are tuned until the model fits. We replace the lottery with a simpler assumption. Every suitable place runs the same complexification process, and the only free quantities are how many such places exist and how many of the lineages they produce expand where we could see them. Using a numerical model of zone abundance, process clocks and expansion, we find the following. If each lineage's clock starts when its planet forms, as an Earth origin of life requires, the empty sky demands that fewer than about one galaxy in fifty million ever produce an expanding civilisation. The lottery returns under another name. If instead lineages share a start, the empty sky allows the first lineages to have reached our level at most about 14 Myr before us. That figure barely moves across ten orders of magnitude of abundance and expansion probability. So the shortest possible lineage is at least 13.59 Gyr, within 0.1% of our own. Finally, only a universal event can synchronise lineages across the galaxies an expanding civilisation could reach in that time. The only sharp universal event early enough is the first carbon chemistry, about 0.2 Gyr after the Big Bang. Common life, an empty sky and no lottery together point to a lineage as old as the chemistry that made it possible.

## 1. Two ways to be early

Humanity appeared 13.8 Gyr after the Big Bang. Stars will keep forming habitable planets for trillions of years, so most observers ought to appear much later than us. Any account of life in the universe has to explain why we are this early. There are two kinds of explanation, and they differ in what our arrival date is taken to measure.

**The lottery.** The hard-steps model (Carter 1983; Watson 2008) treats the emergence of observers as a sequence of $n$ improbable steps, each expected to take longer than a planet's habitable window. Conditioned on success, the chance of finishing by time $t$ grows as $t^n$. Hanson, Martin, McCarter and Paulson (2021) combine this with a deadline: "grabby" civilisations expand, fill the universe within a few Gyr, and prevent later origins inside their volumes. Anyone who exists at all must therefore be early.

The lottery carries two free quantities, and neither has a principled value. The number of steps is read off Earth's history; Hanson et al. put it "near the range 3 to 9", and other authors place it elsewhere (Snyder-Beattie et al. 2021). The overall improbability is not measured at all. Hanson et al. set their birth constant by *assuming* a uniform distribution over our rank among civilisation birth dates. The major evolutionary transitions identified by Maynard Smith and Szathmáry (1995) are real events in our lineage. Nothing in that analysis says each was improbable, and nothing fixes how improbable it was. So under the lottery, the probability that a suitable world produces observers is not an input. It is the residual: the number that reconciles common habitats with an empty sky.

**The process.** The alternative assumes less. Complexity accumulates along suitable trajectories at a rate set by physics, so every suitable place runs the same process and finishes in a characteristic time, not by luck. Two quantities remain free: how many suitable places there are, and what share of the lineages they produce go on to expand visibly. The rest of this note shows that the sky's answer barely depends on either. What it does depend on is when the clocks start.

## 2. The model

We use a deliberately simple scenario model, computed numerically.

- **Suitable zones.** Each galaxy holds $N$ suitable zones today. Our baseline is $10^{10}$: about $10^{11}$ stars, one in ten with a suitable zone. Zones appear at a steady rate from 0.2 Gyr after the Big Bang. One zone hosts one lineage.
- **Process clock.** Every zone runs the same deterministic process. Two ways for its clock to start are considered:
    - *planet-linked*: the clock starts when the zone forms, so older zones finish first;
    - *shared*: all lineages share a start and later zones inherit the accumulated state, so zone age gives no head start.
- **Expansion.** A lineage that reaches our level expands with probability $q$ at speed $v$; our baseline is $v = 0.5c$. A galaxy with $m$ such lineages hosts at least one expander with probability $1-(1-q)^m$.
- **The empty sky.** Galaxies sit at $0.01\ \mathrm{Mpc^{-3}}$ in flat space. Summing over our past light cone gives $\mu$, the expected number of expanded volumes we would see now. We take $P(\text{empty}) = e^{-\mu}$ and report the boundary where an empty sky has probability 5%.

Two kernels are computed: remote visibility, where we would see their expanded volume, and physical arrival, where their front would have reached us. We quote visibility unless stated. The model is conditional: no cosmological expansion, no spread in pace between lineages, ideal visibility. The numbers come from the lineage-cap calculation (commit 8594c5d), in which 31,040 boundaries pass a doubled-resolution integration check.

## 3. If life began on Earth

Suppose each zone's clock starts at its birth, and the process takes as long as it took on Earth, 4.6 Gyr. The oldest zones, born at 0.2 Gyr, then completed at a cosmic age of 4.8 Gyr: 9 Gyr before us. Any of those 9 Gyr of completions that went loud would be in our sky.

The empty sky therefore caps expansion. With $10^{10}$ zones per galaxy, at most $q \approx 2 \times 10^{-18}$ of completed lineages may expand. The arrival kernel gives $2 \times 10^{-17}$, and a capacity-weighted clock gives the same order. The ceiling scales inversely with abundance, so the real constraint is on $qN$. Each galaxy may produce an expanding civilisation with probability no more than about $2 \times 10^{-8}$ over its history: fewer than one galaxy in fifty million.

Planetary starts, common suitable zones and an empty sky are therefore incompatible unless almost every lineage dies, stays home or hides. That is a great filter, and it does the same work as the hard-steps lottery: a probability chosen to fit, with no independent support. Figure 1 shows the conflict directly. With a planetary start, the sky's lower bound on the process duration exceeds Earth's 4.6 Gyr for every $q$ above about $10^{-18}$.

The orange line is Earth's 4.6 Gyr: with a planetary start, every bound above it contradicts Earth's history. Left: elapsed-time clock. ## 4. If lineages share a start

Now let all lineages share a start. A zone's age then gives no head start: zones forming late inherit a lineage whose clock is already running. Completions begin together at a frontier date and then follow the growing number of zones. Our completion is a data point, and the question becomes how far ahead of us the frontier can be.

The answer is short. At $q = 1$, the frontier can be at most **13.7 Myr** ahead of us (27 Myr for physical arrival; 9.6 Myr if the empty sky only needs a 37% probability). It stays the same all the way down to $q = 10^{-6}$. It reaches 16 Myr at $q = 10^{-10}$, and only 63 Myr at $q = 10^{-12}$. The bound is set by geometry, not by abundance. Once every nearby galaxy would host an expander, adding more lineages changes nothing. What matters is how far an expanding volume, or its light, travels during the head start. At 0.5c, 14 Myr is a few megaparsecs: roughly the distance to Andromeda.

So the shortest possible lineage is at least $13.6 - 0.014 \approx$ **13.59 Gyr**. Our lineage ran within about 0.1% of the fastest the universe allows, and that conclusion holds across ten orders of magnitude of the two free quantities. This is the central result. Under the process assumption, an empty sky does not ask how common life is or how often it expands. It tells us how long the process takes.

![Maximum head start of the frontier over us, for shared-start clocks, against $q$ and four abundances (P(empty) = 5% solid, 37% dashed). Once there is about one loud lineage per galaxy ($qN \gtrsim 1$), every curve sits on the same geometric plateau. Left: remote visibility; right: physical arrival.](results/inference/04_head_start_bounds.png){width=100%}

## 5. What could start the clocks together?

A shared start needs a shared cause, and its reach is fixed by the scale found above. Expanding civilisations cross the distances between galaxies quickly. At 0.5c, Andromeda is 5 Myr away and the Virgo cluster about 110 Myr. A synchroniser therefore has to act on every galaxy within a few megaparsecs, and on every galaxy whose light we see, to within about ten million years.

Shared causes come in two kinds:

- **Shared matter.** Trajectories intersect and structured information passes between sites. These events are local. The Sun formed with thousands of siblings in one birth cluster 4.6 Gyr ago. The Milky Way's disk had bursts of star formation 5.7, 1.9 and 1.0 Gyr ago, which coincide with passages of the Sagittarius dwarf (Ruiz-Lara et al. 2020). Each synchronises a cluster or a galaxy at most. After the earliest epoch, matter in different galaxies never shares trajectories.
- **A shared clock.** The same cosmic history unfolds everywhere at about the same time, without contact. Peak star formation around 10 Gyr ago is universal but spread over billions of years. The first stars and the first carbon chemistry, about 0.2 Gyr after the Big Bang, are universal and comparatively sharp.

Only the second kind can reach across galaxies, and only its earliest member is sharp enough. Hence the title. A lineage that is common, synchronised and leaves the sky empty must have started with the first carbon. Any later start needs either a filter or a synchroniser that no one has identified.

One refinement remains open. Even the first-star epoch is not sharp to ten million years: different halos lit up over roughly 100 to 200 Myr. With a spread in start times, the empty sky further requires that our lineage began near the leading edge of that spread. That is a statement about the Milky Way's progenitor halos, and the calculation is in progress.

## 6. What follows

If the argument holds, several things should be true that the lottery does not predict:

- **Lineages run long.** The minimum time to build observers is most of cosmic history. Sharov and Gordon's (2013) extrapolation of genome complexity, to an origin about 9.7 ± 2.5 Gyr ago, is in the same range. Their date would then mark the start of genetic information, not of the lineage.
- **Life elsewhere in the solar system is related to ours.** Shared ancestry, not independent origin.
- **Our neighbourhood was early.** The Milky Way's progenitors formed among the first structures, close to the leading edge of first-star formation.
- **Many near-contemporaries, none far ahead.** Other lineages are reaching our level at about the same time, and their expansion fronts are on their way.

## 7. Assumptions

The conclusion rests on four assumptions.

1. **Expansion is loud.** A civilisation at our level that expands becomes visible. Staying quiet would require every civilisation, every faction within it and every replicator it releases to stay small forever. Under selection, one expander suffices. Mass can be hidden; the entropy production of a large civilisation is harder to hide.
2. **The process is deterministic.** Suitable trajectories complete in the same time, without a lottery. This is the substantive bet. Adding a spread in pace is the next extension.
3. **Information travels with matter.** A shared start needs lineage information to survive transport through grains, planetesimals and comets, and to keep accumulating rather than restart on arrival.
4. **The geometry is simple.** Flat space, homogeneous galaxies, an illustrative galaxy density and ideal visibility. Cosmological expansion and survey sensitivity are extensions.
